newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Ghost of "Think Big" returns to haunt BHP NZ Steel.
newsitem.headline: Ghost of "Think Big" returns to haunt BHP NZ Steel.

text.p: The ghost of New Zealand's so called "Think Big" projects has returned to haunt BHP New Zealand Steel as its Glenbrook mill struggles to survive under the weight of low steel prices and a strong New Zealand dollar.
Analysts said on Wednesday the plant near Auckland would always find it hard to make a profit because it lacked economies of scale.
BHP New Zealand Steel managing director Malcolm Burns said it had only managed small profits in recent years and was currently making a single digit return on capital.
Glenbrook, a product of the 1975-84 interventionist government of the late Sir Robert Muldoon, has had a tumultuous history since opening in the 1970s.

Its capacity was expanded to 775,000 tonnes a year after 1981 when the mill became one of a number of projects intended to scale-up New Zealand's industrial base and create new export-led growth, dubbed the "Think Big" plans.
The government wrote off NZ$1.5 billion (US$1.0 billion) before selling New Zealand Steel in 1987 for NZ$327 million to Alan Hawkins' Equiticorp in a deal that led to Equiticorp's eventual collapse.
BHP bought into the company in 1989 along with Steel and Tube, Fisher and Paykel and ANZ Bank, the giant Australian buying out the others in 1991.
BHP said on Tuesday the plant would survive the next 10 years, at best, but it would probably close sooner, possibly by 1999.
Burns said the mill's size was definitely the issue, but in more ways than one.
"The plant is just too small. In this day and age, a steel company would not build an integrated steel works ... to produce 700,000 tonnes of steel (annually)," he said.

"You probably would not build one unless you were producing at least 3.0 million tonnes of steel. That economy of scale is certainly significant, and there is nothing we can do to overcome that," he said.

But in a sense the plant is also too big for the New Zealand domestic market, forcing it to export more than 66 percent of its output with all the inherent currency risks associated with that. Such a high percentage was almost unheard of in the business, he added.
Furthermore, the concept of taking iron sand and converting it to iron was an unconventional process which made overseas experience inapplicable.
"Commercially, the whole of New Zealand Steel is perhaps a flawed concept rather than just the iron making process, when you add all the things together," he said.
Burns said a 10 percent change in the value of the New Zealand dollar annually would mean a NZ$20-25 million difference to annual export revenue.
"Certainly a 10 percent devaluation would make life a little bit more comfortable. I'm not saying it would be sufficient to save our bacon but it would certainly help," he said.
Analysts said it appeared the mill had fallen prey to the depressed international iron and steel market.
"The world steel market, unless you've got a big state-of-the-art, economies-of-scale plant, you are probably losing money," said one analyst, who declined to be identified. (US$1 = NZ$1.44)
